items.note: Bamboo flute. "kung NAGALINGKOD ang hangin sa sulod sa tubo... ang gitas-on sa NAGALINGKOD nga air column" — lingkod = TO SIT, not to vibrate (mokurog / mag-vibrate). The card's whole mechanism (the air column vibrates) is replaced by 'the air sits inside the tube'; nothing else in the card mentions vibration, and emph_bis even highlights the broken phrase. A child gets no mechanism at all. Corpus's own correct words appear in other cards (mokurog in ffct-25334/25335, nag-vibrate in ffct-25392/25395/25398).

Marimba/xylophone. "Ang mas taas nga bar NAGALINGKOD nga hinay... ang mas mubo NAGALINGKOD nga paspas" — 'sits slowly / sits fast'. The entire answer to the question (long bars vibrate slowly = lower pitch) is destroyed; vibration is never named anywhere else in the card.

Kulintang gongs. "...mas ubos nga pitch tungod kay NAGALINGKOD nga mas hinay" — the causal clause that answers the headline question ('because they vibrate more slowly') becomes 'because they sit more slowly'. No other vibration word in the card, so the reason is unrecoverable.

Eardrum. "Kung matahasan sa mga sound wave, NALINGKOD kini sama sa panit sa tinuod nga tambol" — 'it sits like the skin of a real drum'. The single fact the card exists to teach (the eardrum vibrates when sound hits it) is gone; the card never says mokurog/vibrate.

Cochlea. "Kung NAGALINGKOD sila, nagapadala sila og electrical signals sa utok" — 'when they sit'. The trigger for the hair cells firing (vibration) is replaced by sitting, and vibration appears nowhere else in the Cebuano, so the conversion mechanism is lost.

title_bis "Bentilador BAHU Singaw Presko" for title_en 'Fan Sweat Evaporation'. bahu = ODOUR/stink in Cebuano, not sweat (singot). Confirmed false-friend class, and the card's own body uses the correct word ('mas paspas mosingaw ang singot'), so the title is the outlier — it tells the child a fan works on smell.

title_bis "Canals sa BALI" for title_en 'Semicircular Balance Canals'. bali = BROKEN/fracture (or to flip over) in Cebuano; balance is balanse/timbang. The body has it right ('aron mabalanse ka'), so the title is the outlier and reads as 'canals of the broken'.

"Kung ibutang ang DAYAMI sa baso sa tubig" plus title_bis 'Kurbado nga Dayami'. dayami = rice straw/hay, not a drinking straw (istro/straw); the English polysemy was resolved the wrong way. Both title and body use it and nothing corrects it, so the child is told to put hay in a glass of water rather than the drinking straw the demonstration depends on.

"Sa BAKAL ang tunog mobalhin og mga 5,100 m/s" — bakal = TO BUY in Cebuano; steel/iron is puthaw or landok. This is the sentence that carries the 5,100 m/s figure, so the number is attached to a verb ('in buying') rather than a material. Only the keyword title ('Tunog Malaksi Landok Solido') has the right word — weak repair for the load-bearing fact sentence.

"wool" is rendered "lana" in BOTH the title ("Lana Hangin Insulator") and the body question ("Nganong ang lana ug nakulong nga hangin nagpabilin og mainit?"). In Cebuano lana = COCONUT OIL (Tagalog lana = wool); Cebuano wool is balhibo sa karnero / delana. The card never says wool anywhere, and the follow-up "gigamit kini sa damit ug bubong sa balay" reinforces the false reading: a child learns that OIL is a great insulator used in clothing and roofing. Nothing in the card restores wool.

"particles vibrate perpendicular" becomes "ang mga particle NAGALINGKOD perpendicular" — lingkod = to SIT. The card is the definition of a transverse wave, so the verb IS the fact: as written it says the particles sit still (static) rather than oscillate, which is the opposite of wave motion. The card never uses mokurog/mag-vibrate anywhere to restore it. (Same mistranslation recurs in ffct-25507 "Dali kining nagalingkod" for vibrating vocal cords, but there the short/thin-cords -> high-pitch fact still survives, so only this one is flagged.)

Title "Timbangan sa Bukal" for "Spring Balance": in Cebuano bukal = TO BOIL (this same batch uses it that way three times — pagbukal/nagbukal/mobukal sa tubig), and a water spring is tubod (used correctly in ffct-25532's title "Mainit nga Tubod"). Bukal is never a mechanical coil spring in either language. The card's OWN body and emph_bis use the right word, "tinggol" — the title is the outlier, reading as "boiling scale".

"Mix every paint colour together" becomes "PAGKAT-ON nimo ang tanang kolor sa pintura" — pagkat-on = to LEARN. The card's entire fact is what happens when you MIX all paints; as written the cause is learning the colours, and neither the rest of the body nor the title ("Tanan Pintura Putik Mug-it") ever says mix/sagol. A child cannot answer "what happens when you mix all the paint colours?" from this card, and is told a false causal chain (learning colours -> they absorb wavelengths).

"Metals like iron" becomes "Ang mga metal sama sa BAKAL" — bakal = TO BUY in Cebuano (iron is puthaw); it is on the confirmed false-friend list for this corpus. The clause reads as "metals such as buying", and the card's named exemplar of a metal is destroyed with no correction anywhere in the card (it only says "metal" and "metal nga kutsara"). Lower severity than the others since the headline fact (metals heat fast) survives; flagged because it is a confirmed swap and the card never supplies puthaw. Note ffct-25451 has the same word ("pabrika sa bakal" for steel factories) but there it is a peripheral detail and the pyrometer fact is fully intact, so it is left as a PASS.

EN: "Light scatters off tiny particles in the air like dust or smoke, making the beam visible!" BIS: "Ang suga nagawagtang sa gagmayng particles sa hangin sama sa abog o usok, makita ang beam!" In Cebuano wagtang is to remove/make vanish — the corpus uses it that way on all 28 cards (sabon nagwagtang sa mikrobyo, pagwagtang sa plema). A Cebuano-only child is taught the opposite mechanism: the light DESTROYS the dust, rather than bouncing off it. Scattering is the whole content of the Tyndall card, and nothing in the Cebuano restores it (the siblings ffct-25296/25478 carry the same swap for Rayleigh scattering).

EN: "your voice is made by vibrating vocal cords." BIS: "ang imong boses gihimo sa nagalingkod nga vocal cords." Lingkod is to SIT — 85 corpus cards use it only that way (naglingkod, molingkod sa iyang mga itlog), while vibrate is mouyog/mokurog, which this same batch uses correctly (ffct-25582 nagakurog, ffct-25586 mauyog, ffct-25588 nag-uyog). The card's single teaching claim becomes "your voice is made by seated vocal cords"; the earlier sentence only says to feel a vibration at the throat, never that the cords are what vibrates.

Title BIS "Si Isaac Newton Tulo Bala" for title EN "Newton's Laws Author": bala is a BULLET in Cebuano (all 7 corpus uses are bullets — pusil/kanyon recoil cards), so the title a child scans reads "Isaac Newton three bullets". Law is balaod, which the card's own body uses correctly ("ang tulo ka balaod sa paglihok") and which 20 other titles use (incl. ffct-25680 in this same batch, "Tulo ka Balaod ni Newton"). Title-only defect, same class as the asin/aso finding.

Title BIS "1687 Principia Bala Kalihukan" for title EN "1687 Principia Published": reads as "1687 Principia bullet motion" — bala is bullet, not balaod (law). The body is correct ("ang iyang mga balaod sa paglihok"), so the title is the outlier; corpus-wide only 4 titles make this swap against 20 that write balaod.

EN: "They absorb light when the room is bright and slowly release it in the dark!" BIS: "Nagsipsip sila og suga kung hayag ug hinay-hinay ginhawa sa kangitngit!" Ginhawa is breath/to breathe — all 93 corpus uses are breathing; release is mopagawas/magbuhi (34 cards). The object (the stored light) is also dropped, so the Cebuano answer never says the stars give the light back out; the child is told they "slowly breathe in the dark", and phosphorescence is left unexplained.

EN: "James Watt greatly improved the steam engine". BIS glosses it as "steam engine (makina nga gipalihok sa aso)" — aso in Cebuano is SMOKE, not steam (alisngaw/singaw). The gloss is the only Cebuano explanation of what drives the engine, and nothing in the card corrects it, so a Cebuano-only child learns a steam engine is smoke-powered. The corpus's own convention contradicts it: ffct-25820 and ffct-25821 (same batch, same topic) both say "makinang de-singaw", and ffct-25763 uses "alisngaw" correctly for steam.

EN: "A screw makes it easier to hold two things together or lift things; it turns a twisting motion into a strong forward force". BIS: "...paghugpong sa duha ka butang o PAGPATAAS SA TUBIG" — "lift things" became "raise WATER". Different referent, never corrected anywhere in the card; the card teaches the child that a screw's second use is raising water (an Archimedes screw), not lifting objects generally. The same clause also drops "forward" from "strong forward force" ("kusog nga puwersa" only), so the direction of the converted force is gone too.

title_bis "Fahrenheit Buhag Scale" for title_en "Fahrenheit Scale Maker". "Buhag" is not Cebuano for maker/creator (that is naghimo / magbubuhat); it looks like a corruption of "buhat" and as written carries no usable meaning, so the title alone does not say that Fahrenheit MADE the scale. The card's own body uses the correct word — "ang naghimo sa Fahrenheit temperature scale" — which is what marks the title as the outlier. Lowest-confidence of the three: the body does restore the fact, so this is a title-standalone defect, not a body falsehood.

title_bis "Mohs Scale Kagwang Mineral Bato" for "Mohs Measures Hardness". Kagwang is the Philippine flying lemur/colugo, an ANIMAL, not a property - the same corpus uses it that way (ffct-00185 title_bis "Kagwang"/title_en "Colugo"; ffct-01101 "Ang kagwang o Philippine flying lemur"). Cebuano for hardness is katig-a, and this card's OWN body uses it correctly ("kung paila ka katig-a ang bato", "nagsukod sa hardness sa mga mineral") - strongest evidence the title is the outlier. A child sees a rock-hardness card headed with an animal's name.

en "The cheetah is the absolute fastest LAND animal on Earth" -> bis "Ang cheetah mao ang pinakapaspas nga hayop sa tibuok yuta" = "the fastest animal in the whole world". The load-bearing qualifier "land" is gone and the Cebuano sentence is simply false (a peregrine falcon is far faster). Only the keyword-salad title ("Cheetah 110 km/h Yuta Hayop") hints at "land animal", and a sibling card in the corpus keeps it properly ("Cheetah Labing Malaksi Yuta"). A Cebuano-only child ends up believing the cheetah is the fastest animal that exists.

title_bis "Videophone Nawong Kausab" for title_en "Zara Videophone Face Call". Kausab/kausaban means CHANGE in Cebuano and is used that way throughout the corpus ("kausaban sa klima" = climate change, "makausab og kolor" = can change colour), so the title reads "Videophone Face Change" - a different thing from showing the face of the person you are talking to. The body's repair word is itself not Cebuano ("nawong sa imong kausap" is Tagalog; Cebuano is kaistorya), so neither field names the referent correctly; only the trailing "sama ra sa video call karon" rescues the fact.

title_bis "James Watt Steam Engine Pahuwat" for title_en "Watt Improved the Engine": pahuwat is from huwat/hulat = to wait (make someone wait), not pauswag/pagpalambo = to improve. The headline therefore reads "James Watt steam engine, make-wait" — the card's key verb (improved, not invented) is replaced by an unrelated action. The card's own body uses the correct word ("Gipalambo niya ang steam engine niadtong 1760s ug 1770s"), which is the evidence the title is the outlier; a child who reads only the title gets no fact at all from it.

title_bis "Bullet Train Shinkansen 320" states 320 km/h, but the English title carries no number and both the en and bis bodies say ~300 km/h ("mga 300 ka kilometro kada oras"). The Cebuano-only child gets two conflicting speeds for the same fact from one card, and the title — the part scanned first and remembered — is the wrong one. Number invented/changed in translation; en title is just "Bullet Trains' Speed".

title_bis "Pamalandong sa Hayag" for title_en "Light Reflection". In Cebuano pamalandong = meditation/contemplation (root landong = shadow/shade), never optical reflection; a child reading the title alone gets "meditating on light" or "shadowing of light" - the opposite of light bouncing off a surface. The card's own body uses the correct concept ("Ang reflection mao ang pagbalik sa kahayag gikan sa usa ka surface sama sa samin") and never uses pamalandong, which is the outlier evidence that the title is the defect. Correct options: Repleksyon sa Kahayag, or Pagbanaag sa Kahayag. Corpus check: pamalandong occurs in the Cebuano corpus only in the ponder sense ("mipamalandong si Junrey").

EN: "generate static electricity just by rubbing a balloon to transfer electrons". BIS: "Makagama ka og static electricity pinaagi ra sa pag-uyog og balloon aron ma-transfer ang mga electron!" — uyog means TO SHAKE in Cebuano (rub = kuskos). Shaking a balloon does not transfer electrons or charge hair; the card teaches a method that does not work. Nothing else in the card (title "Static Elektrisidad", question about making hair stand up) restores the rubbing action, so the fact is unrecoverable from the Cebuano.

EN: "Sitting near a campfire warms your skin!" BIS: "Mokusog ang panit nimo kung maglingkod duol sa campfire!" — mokusog = becomes STRONG/intensifies, not moinit (warms). The remaining sentence only says the wood emits infrared radiation that passes through the air (it also drops "to reach you"), so the card never states that the fire warms you. A child reads that a campfire makes their skin strong — false, and the actual heat-radiation-warms-you point is unrecoverable.

EN: "The Stanley Classic vacuum bottle KEEPS liquids hot using a vacuum layer between its walls to block heat conduction". BIS: "GIPAINIT sa Stanley Classic vacuum bottle ang mga likido gamit ang vacuum layer..." — gipainit = heats/makes hot, i.e. the bottle is described as heating the liquid rather than keeping already-hot liquid hot (gipabiling init). Nothing in the card corrects it, so a child concludes a vacuum flask heats drinks via its vacuum layer, which is physically false.

"Slippery" is rendered as maligid (= to ROLL / be rolled) in BOTH the question and the conclusion, and nothing on the card corrects it: "Nganong maligid kaayo ang nabasa nga dahon sa saging? ... Mao nga maligid kaayo kini kung mabasa." Title ("Dahon sa Saging") drops the property entirely. A Cebuano-only child is told a wet banana leaf ROLLS a lot -- a different, false claim -- and never learns it is slippery; the surviving "nagpakunhod sa friction" gives the cause but not the observable fact the card is about. Corpus evidence this is an outlier, not regional usage: madulas is used for slippery 70x across the sweep batches, madanglog/maligid never -- every other maligid in the corpus means rolling ("maligid sa lamesa", "maligid lang kini sa ehe", "maligid sa kabayo ang bug-at nga karga"). Note ffct-27102 pairs "madulas ug maligid" for "slipping and sliding", which is fine; this card is the one where maligid stands alone for slippery.

EN "a simple iron nail" -> BIS "ang pako nga puthaw". In Cebuano pako = WING (same batch, ffct-27241, correctly uses "ang mga pako niini" for a paper airplane's wings); Cebuano for nail is LANSANG, which is what the rest of the corpus uses for exactly this experiment (ffct-22579 "paglukot ug kawad sa lansang", ffct-24053, ffct-26540, ffct-13172). The card never says lansang anywhere, so the only object a child is given is an "iron wing" to wrap with wire - the whole hands-on fact (wrap wire around a NAIL to make an electromagnet) is unrecoverable from the Cebuano.

EN "Why are the rocks on the Mayon Volcano trail rough? The rough volcanic rocks increase friction..." -> BIS "Ngano nga GARBO ang mga bato... Ang GARBONG nga volcanic rocks...". Cebuano garbo = PRIDE/elegance (corpus ffct-05090: "Garbo sa Palawan ang tandikan" = Palawan is proud of the tandikan); rough is gaspang/magaspang (corpus ffct-04122 "gaspang ang panit sa pagi", ffct-28006 title "Magaspang Kennon Road"). The wrong word is used in BOTH the question and the answer, so roughness - the property that causes the friction - is never stated; the child is asked why rocks are "proud" and cannot answer the card's own question.

EN "A fully drawn bow stores about 50 joules of elastic potential energy" -> BIS "Kung hingpit nga GIHUYOP ang bow...". Huyop = TO BLOW throughout the corpus (95 hits, all blowing/wind: ffct-05080 elephant blowing air, ffct-16287 wind blowing). Nothing in the card says the bow is pulled or bent, so the stated condition for storing the elastic energy is a false one (blowing a bow). Compare ffct-24843, which states the same physics correctly: "Ang pana nga kawayan MOBALUKTOT aron magtipig og elastic potential energy".

EN "When you touch its sensitive trigger hairs, it quickly changes into kinetic energy to snap shut" -> BIS "Kung MAHIPOS ang sensitive trigger hairs niini, dali kaayo kining mo-convert ngadto sa kinetic energy." Hipos = to put away / tidy / gather (corpus ffct-08734 "gihipos... ang liso" = collected the seeds); touch is hikap/tandog. The trigger condition is replaced by a nonsense one and the BIS also drops "to snap shut", so nothing in the card restores what actually makes the trap close - a child cannot answer what triggers the Venus flytrap.

"ang pako nga puthaw" for "an iron nail". In Cebuano pako = WING (or the edible fern); nail is lansang. This is the Tagalog false friend (Tagalog pako = nail). The card never says lansang anywhere, so the Cebuano-only reader is told a magnet attracts an "iron wing" and not an aluminum can — the object the whole demonstration rests on is a different thing.

Same swap: "chemical reaction sa metal nga pako" for "chemical reaction with metal nails" in the lemon-battery card. pako = wing in Cebuano (lansang = nail); nothing in the card restores it, so the child cannot reproduce or picture the setup that makes the lemon generate electricity.

title_bis "Tunog Bakal 15 Beses" for "Sound Steel 15x Faster". bakal in Cebuano = TO BUY (Tagalog bakal = iron/steel; Cebuano is puthaw / asero) — a confirmed false friend in this corpus. The title is the outlier: this card's own body keeps "steel" in English, and ffct-27473 in the same batch correctly uses "puthaw".

title_bis "Magnet Nickel Cobalt Bakal" uses bakal for the iron of "Magnets Pull Nickel Cobalt Too". Again bakal = to buy in Cebuano, not iron (puthaw). Body evidence that the title is the outlier: this card's body writes "iron" in English and the parallel card ffct-27473 writes "Dili lang puthaw ang gidani sa mga magnet".

The payload fact is reversed into a hedge: EN "It ONLY changes the direction of your pull" becomes "Usahay lang niya usbon ang direksyon" = "it only SOMETIMES changes the direction". A fixed pulley always redirects the pull — that is its entire function — so the Cebuano-only child learns something false and cannot answer what a fixed pulley does. Compounded by "kusog nga imong pagahikap" (hikap = to TOUCH) for "lifting effort" and "pag-uyog" (uyog = to SHAKE) for "your pull"; nothing in the card restores either.

The question asks "Ngano nga MALUSPAD ang paglakaw sa basa nga nahulog nga dahon sa mangga?" — luspad = PALE / faded, not slippery (madanglog/madulas). Slipperiness is the effect the whole card explains and it appears nowhere else in the card, so a Cebuano-only child is asked why walking on wet mango leaves is "pale" and never learns that low friction makes you slip. Sibling card ffct-27392 uses "madulas" correctly, which is what this card needed.

Safety card whose verb is wrong in both title and body. Body: "Kanunay nga PAGGUKOD ang plastic plug" — gukod = to CHASE / run after, not to pull (bira). Title: "BATI-A ang Plug Dili Kable" — bati = to feel/hear, not pull. The card is an instruction, and the instruction "pull the plug, not the cord" is never actually stated in Cebuano, so the child cannot perform the action the card exists to teach.

"ang kabayo nga nagdagan ug NAGGUKOD sa kalesa" for "a galloping horse PULLING a kalesa". gukod = to chase; pulling/hauling is guyod or bira. This reverses the relationship — the horse is now running after the kalesa instead of drawing it — and nothing in the card corrects it. Same wrong verb as ffct-27438, so it is a repeated swap rather than a one-off typo.

title_bis "Grabidad sa Lawak" for "Gravity in Space". In Cebuano lawak = a ROOM / chamber; outer space is kalawakan or kawanangan (Tagalog lawak = expanse — the false-friend route). Corpus evidence that this title is the outlier: ffct-27367 titles the same concept "Kahayag sa Kalawakan" and ffct-27399 asks "Mawala ba ang gravity sa KALAWAKAN?". The title as written reads "Gravity in the Room".

Body calls the wheelbarrow "bangko" (bench/stool) twice, including the core claim "Ang bangko usa ka klase sa lever" — a child learns a BENCH is a lever that lifts soil. Cebuano for wheelbarrow is kariton, which this corpus uses correctly in ffct-27562 and ffct-27589, and even in this card's own title_bis ("Kariton Lever Yuta"), so the body is the outlier and the sentence it breaks is the card's whole fact.

title_bis "Tunog nga Bulong" — bulong is Cebuano for MEDICINE/remedy (Tagalog false friend: Tagalog bulong = whisper). The card is "Whispering Sound", so the title reads "Medicine Sound". The card's OWN body uses the correct Cebuano "hunghog" (hunghong = whisper), which confirms the title is the outlier.

"mas luspad kini kaysa sa dry rubber" — luspad means PALE/faded (colour), not slippery (madanglog/madulas). The card's only conclusion becomes "ice is paler than dry rubber", so a child reads friction 0.03 vs 0.8 as a statement about colour. Nothing else in the card (title "Yelo Friction 0.03") restores slipperiness; sibling card ffct-27485 states the same fact with "kadulas".

Both the question and the answer use "makatalikod" (to turn one's back) for "jump": "Nganong makatalikod ug unom ka beses nga mas taas ang astronaut sa Buwan?" The card's whole point — you can JUMP six times higher under 1/6 gravity — is replaced by an unrelated action and never restored (lukso never appears); ffct-27582 uses "naglukso-lukso" correctly for the same Moon-gravity fact.

title_bis "Pamalandong" is reflection in the MEDITATION/introspection sense only; optical reflection is never called pamalandong in Cebuano. The card is about white Boracay sand reflecting sunlight, and its own body uses "Nag-reflect" (also the emph_bis term), so the title names a different thing than every other field in the card.

"Mokurot ang suga pag-sulod sa tubig" — kurot means to PINCH, not to bend (liko/bawog). This is the card's explanation for the broken-looking straw and it is the highlighted emph_bis phrase, so the refraction mechanism a child is meant to take away is replaced by "light pinches"; nothing else in the card states that light bends.

EN: electromagnet 'generates enough magnetic force to LIFT an entire crushed car (1,500 kg)'. BIS: 'makapahimo og igong magnetic force aron BUHIAN ang tibuok nga gisi nga sakyanan' — buhian = to RELEASE / let go, the opposite of alsahon (lift). The card's whole point (a magnet can pick up a 1,500 kg car) is reversed into the magnet letting the car go, and nothing else in the card supplies 'lift'.

EN: holding hot pumice 'WARMS your hands through direct heat conduction'. BIS: 'mokusog ang imong mga kamot' = your hands become STRONG (kusog = strength), not moinit/mopainit (become warm). A child reads that holding a hot rock makes your hands strong — a false claim, and the actual fact (heat transfers into your hands) is never stated anywhere on the card.

EN: 'Does a loud shout travel faster than a quiet WHISPER?' BIS: 'kusog nga singgit kaysa sa hilum nga HUNONG?' — hunong = to STOP/halt; whisper is hunghong. The second item of the comparison stops being a sound at all, so the card's point (loudness does not change sound speed) is unanswerable from the Cebuano; the body never repeats the correct word.

EN: scrap-yard electromagnets 'temporarily attract and LIFT heavy pieces of discarded iron and steel'. BIS: 'temporaryong makaakit ug MAKABUG-AT og discarded iron ug steel' — makabug-at = can MAKE HEAVY, not makaalsa (can lift). As written the card asserts that magnets make scrap iron heavy, and the lifting fact is gone from the card.

title_bis 'Pamalandong' for title_en 'Reflection'. Pamalandong is mental reflection / contemplation (palandong = to ponder); optical reflection is repleksyon / pagsalamin. The title names a completely different thing — and the card's own body uses the correct sense ('ang ambient light NAG-REFLECT sa iyang nawong'), which is the evidence the title is the outlier. This is the English-homonym trap, not compact title style.

Same defect as ffct-27757: title_bis 'Pamalandong' for title_en 'Mirror Reflection'. Pamalandong = meditation/contemplation, never optical reflection (repleksyon / pagsalamin sa samin). Here the body never supplies the correct word either — it only describes light bouncing ('ang kahayag mobalik-balik tali kanila') — so the Cebuano title label for mirror reflection is simply wrong.

title_bis 'Malisod nga Yelo' for title_en 'Slippery Ice'. Malisod = DIFFICULT (lisod); slippery is madanlog/madanglog. The title names a different property than the card teaches, and the body uses the correct sense (the English loan 'mas slippery kaysa goma'), marking the title as the outlier.

EN: rough abaca rope's high friction "stops them from slipping" when fishermen tie bangka to docks. BIS: "Mao nga dili sila maluspad kung ang mga mangingisda magtali..." — luspad = PALE / FADED, not slip (danlog / madulas / madalin-as). The Cebuano therefore teaches that high friction keeps the rope from fading in colour, which is false, and the slipping fact — the whole point of the card — appears nowhere else in the card. Same-batch evidence that the corpus knows the right word: ffct-27821, ffct-27885, ffct-27893 and ffct-27902 all use madulas/pagdulas/danlog correctly for slipping; this card's own body already uses magaspang correctly for 'rough', so maluspad is the lone outlier.

title_bis "Pamalandong" for title_en "Light Reflection". Palandong/pamalandong in Cebuano = MEDITATION, pondering, contemplation — the mental sense of English "reflection", never the optical one (pagsalamin / banaag / 'reflection'). A child sees a card titled "Meditation" over a card about capiz shells bouncing light. The body never repairs it in Cebuano: it only says "nag-reflect sila og kusog nga kahayag", i.e. the English loanword, so the wrong Cebuano sense is never corrected.

title_bis "Hilom nga Kahangturan" for title_en "Silent Outer Space". Kahangturan = ETERNITY / forever (time), not outer space (kawanangan / kalawakan). The title names a different thing and the body only uses the English "outer space", so no Cebuano word ever restores it. Same batch proves the correct word is available: ffct-27810 is titled "Tunog sa Kawanangan" for "Sound in Space".

EN: "The ROUGH BARK of a narra tree increases friction". BIS: "Ang garbong kahoy sa narra tree nagdugang friction" — garbo in Cebuano = PRIDE / elegance / flair, so this reads "the elegant wood of the narra". Two losses that are never restored: the mechanism (surface roughness is why friction is high — the only science the card carries) and panit/bark becomes kahoy/wood. A child reading only the Cebuano cannot answer "why don't the insects slip?" with anything but "because narra wood". Correct word is magaspang, which this very batch uses properly in ffct-27872.

Same swap as ffct-27821: EN "The ROUGH TEXTURE of a dried coconut husk (bunot) increases friction" → BIS "Ang garbong texture sa uga nga panit sa lubi (bunot) nagdugang og friction", i.e. "the elegant/proud texture". Nothing in the card restores 'rough' in Cebuano, so the reason bunot grips and scrubs is gone. Flagged with slightly lower confidence than ffct-27821 because 'texture ... nagdugang og friction' still gets the child partway to the answer — but the wrong word is the same real Cebuano word meaning something else, and the fix is the same (magaspang).

"Magnet & Nail" / "iron nail" becomes "bakal nga pako" in BOTH the title_bis ("Magnet ug Pako") and the body (twice). In Cebuano pako = WING (nail is lansang), and bakal = TO BUY (iron is puthaw — this same batch uses puthaw correctly in ffct-27958 and ffct-27998). Nothing in the card restores it, so the child reads "what happens when a magnet comes near a buy-wing" and never learns the object is an iron nail. The whole probe (magnetic domains in iron) is unanswerable.

Outcome reversed: "Kung isira nimo ang switch, moagi ang electrical energy sa wire aron MAPALONG ang bombilya" = closing the switch makes the bulb GO OUT. EN is "to light the bulb". Palong = extinguish — confirmed inside this same batch, where ffct-27935 uses "mapalong ang tanang suga" for "all the lights go out". The answer sentence teaches the opposite of the circuit fact; the question header ("pagpailaw") only makes it contradictory, not recoverable.

Two substitutions gut the card. (1) "Ang GARBONG nga texture sa abaca fibers mopataas sa friction" — garbo = pride/elegance, not rough; the correct word magaspang is used in ffct-28006's own title for the identical "rough surface increases friction" fact, so the causal reason (roughness) is simply absent here and the title ("Friction sa Abaka") restores nothing. (2) "maayo kini gamiton sa PAG-UKIT sa bug-at nga karga" — ukit = to carve/engrave; EN is "tying heavy loads" (paghigot/pagbugkos), so the application fact is replaced by a different thing. A child reads that abaca's elegant texture is good for carving heavy loads.

EN: gumamela "has bright red petals". BIS: "adunay hayag nga pula nga mga talong" — talong is an EGGPLANT, not a petal (Cebuano petal = petalo / mga dahon sa bulak). The card then says "Nag-reflect KINI sa red light wavelengths", so the red eggplants are also the thing that reflects red light and attracts butterflies. Nothing in the card (title is only "Pula Gumamela") restores "petal", so a child reading only the Cebuano learns that a hibiscus grows red eggplants.

Tagalog false friend, and it is in the TITLE as well as the body: title_bis "Pagmamagnet sa Pako" and body "temporary magnet gikan sa pako nga puthaw". In Cebuano pako = WING (pakô) / edible FERN (pakû); a nail is lansang. The whole card is an instruction about an iron nail, and the word is never corrected anywhere in the card — the child is told to stroke an iron wing with a magnet.

Same false friend, and here it breaks a hands-on instruction: "Isuksok ang copper nga pako ug zinc nga pako sa gipiga nga calamansi" for "pop a copper nail and a zinc nail into a squeezed calamansi". Cebuano pako = wing/fern (nail = lansang). The card never names the object any other way, so a child cannot carry out or picture the calamansi-battery demo.

Third instance of the same swap: "makadani sa mga pako nga puthaw" for "attracts iron nails". Cebuano pako = wing/fern, not lansang (nail). The contrast with aluminum and copper survives, but the object the magnet picks up is named as an iron wing and is never corrected in the card.

EN: the electric ray "generates sudden electrical currents to STUN small fish before eating them". BIS: "nagpagawas og kalit nga electrical currents aron PATINDOG ang gagmay nga isda una kaunon" — patindog = to make (something) STAND UP / erect. The effect of the shock is the whole point of the card, and the Cebuano states a different effect that nothing else in the card corrects (stun = palipong / paralisahon).

title_bis "Sip-sip nga Lever" for "Seesaw Lever": sip-sip in Cebuano means to SUCK/sip, it is not a seesaw. Strongest evidence the title is the outlier: this card's own body keeps the English word ("kahoy nga seesaw sa Rizal Park") and the sibling card ffct-28120 also keeps "seesaw". The title names a different object; the body is fine.

title_bis "Kulob Room Temp" for "Boiling at Room Temp": Cebuano kulob = lying FACE-DOWN / overturned; to boil is kulo. The card's own body has the correct verb ("pwede MOKULO sa room temperature"), which is exactly the pattern of a title outlier — the title heading the boiling-at-room-temperature fact says something about being upside-down instead.

title_bis "Lubog Niyog Shell" for "Coconut Fall Shells": lubog in Cebuano means MURKY/turbid (Tagalog: submerged/sunken) — it does not mean falling. The body has the correct word ("samtang NAGAHULOG", "nagbira ... paingon sa ilawom"), and the rest of this batch uses lubi for coconut (ffct-28106, ffct-28148, ffct-28217) while only this title uses the Tagalog niyog — both signs the title is the outlier.

EN: "gravity is the PULLING force that makes precipitation fall". BIS: "ang gravity mao ang puwersa nga NAGAHUYOP" — huyop = to BLOW (with breath/air). The card's science point is that gravity pulls; the Cebuano states the opposite kind of force (blowing/pushing air) and never says bira/dani anywhere, unlike the neighbouring gravity cards (ffct-28107 "i-pull", ffct-28110 "gipull", ffct-28159 "nagbira"). Lower confidence than the flags above because the clause "precipitation mohulog gikan sa panganod paingon sa yuta" still keeps the downward direction.

The card asks "Unsa ang fluid friction o drag?" and the EN answer is "It occurs when objects move through liquids like water or gases like air, SLOWING THEM DOWN!" The Cebuano stops at "kung ang mga butang molihok sa likido sama sa tubig o gas sama sa hangin!" and drops the slowing-down effect entirely — the defining property the card exists to teach. A child reading only the Cebuano cannot answer what drag actually does.

title_bis "Iridocytes sa Tahong" names TAHONG = green mussel, a different animal from the giant clam (taklobo) the card is about. The card's own body keeps the correct thing ("Ang mga dako nga clam sa coral reef") and the terms are literally "giant clams" — so the title is the outlier. A child reading the title learns that mussels have iridocytes and host algae, which is false.

"Ang short circuit MOPASULOD sa normal nga electrical path" says the short circuit ENTERS / feeds into the normal electrical path — the reverse of the English "bypasses the normal electrical path" (should be molaktaw / molikay). The definitional fact of the card (a short circuit skips the normal path) is inverted and never corrected anywhere on the card; only the consequence (unrestricted flow, melting heat) survives.

title_bis "Utak Binti Bulan Sulti" drops BULAN = MOON into a card about the brain telling the leg to kick a soccer ball. Nothing in the en/bis body or terms mentions the moon (body is correct: utok -> electrical impulses -> kalamnan sa tiil). Looks like a corruption of "bola"; as shipped the title names a thing that is not in the card.

Body uses "makapahuyop" twice for levitate/float — HUYOP = to blow (with breath), not to float (palutaw). Both the question and the answer become "can a magnet make a live frog blow?", so the body never states the card's only fact (a 45-Tesla field can levitate a live frog). Recoverable ONLY from the one-word keyword title ("...Palaka Lutaw"); drop this flag if title-restoration counts as recovery.

"ang metal nga kutsara MOKUSOG sa nagbukal nga sabaw" = the spoon becomes strong/intense, not hot (moinit). The card's concrete claim — the metal spoon GETS HOT in boiling soup — is never stated in Cebuano; a child has to infer it from the general warm->cool sentence before it.

title_bis "Pamalandong sa Hayag" for "Light Reflection": pamalandong is contemplation/meditation, the mental sense of "reflection", not light bouncing (salamin/pagbanaag). The card's own body keeps the optical sense ("Sa reflection stage sa vision, mopakpak ang light rays..."), and sibling cards in this batch use physical phrasing (ffct-28394 "Salamin sa Flip", ffct-28523 "Nabalik nga Kahayag"), so the title is the outlier. A child reading the title alone is told the card is about pondering, not about light.

Body question reads "Nganong maka-tulon ka ug taas sa luksong-tinik?" — tulon in Cebuano is TO SWALLOW; jump is lukso (Tagalog-interference from talon). The card's own title_bis ("Paglukso ug Grabidad") uses lukso correctly, which is the strongest evidence the body verb is the defect. The card's question sentence asks why you can swallow high.

"Ang fiberglass insulation nag-trapo sa hangin" for "traps air": trapo is a rag / to wipe, so the Cebuano says the insulation WIPES the air. The trapped-air mechanism is the card's only explanation of why heat transfer slows, and nothing else in the card restores it. Compare ffct-28426 in the same batch, which writes the verb correctly as "pag-trap".

title_bis "SA Node Kasing" — kasing on its own is a SPINNING TOP in Cebuano; the heart is kasingkasing. The body uses kasingkasing correctly twice, so the truncated title names a different object. This is a title-only wrong word, not compact-title style, because the shortened form is itself a real and different Cebuano noun.

title_bis "Vigan Luto Malamig" for "Vigan Cool Brick Walls": malamig is Tagalog (Cebuano is bugnaw, which the card's own body uses), and luto in Cebuano means COOKED, not brick (tisa/ladrilyo). The title reads roughly "Vigan Cooked Cold" and names neither walls nor bricks; only the body carries the fact.

"gihurot sa gravity ang flying fish pabalik sa tubig" for "gravity pulls the flying fish back down": hurot means to use up / finish off / wipe out, not to pull (bira/butong). The card's single claim is what gravity DOES to the fish, and the verb names consumption rather than a downward pull; nothing elsewhere in the card supplies the correct verb.

Direction reversal. EN: kalesa shafts "help the horse easily PULL the heavy carriage"; BIS: "Nagtabang kini sa kabayo nga PAGDUSO sa bug-at nga kariton" = help the horse PUSH it. `duso` is push in Cebuano (same corpus uses `iduso` for English "push" in ffct-28638, and `gibira` for a horse pulling a tartanilla in ffct-28628). Nothing in this card restores "pull", and push-vs-pull is the exact force concept the card teaches, so a Cebuano-only reader learns the wrong direction.

Medium confidence. EN: "Your vocal cords VIBRATE to produce sound waves"; BIS: "Ang imong vocal cords MOBATI ug maghimo og sound waves". `bati` means to feel/greet (or bad/ugly) in Cebuano, never to vibrate (`mokurog`/`mo-uyog`). The vibration mechanism is unrecoverable from this card; its two near-duplicates ffct-28570 and ffct-28638 both use `mo-vibrate` correctly, so this card is the outlier. Flagged as lower severity because the rest of the sentence (sound waves travel through air to be heard) still lands.

title_bis "X-ray Buto" for "X-rays See Bones": buto is the TAGALOG word for bone. In Cebuano bone is bukog; buto means an explosion/blast (and carries a vulgar sense). The card's own body uses bukog correctly three times ("imong mga bukog", "masuhop sa mas baga nga bukog", "litrato sa mga bukog"), which is the strongest evidence the title is the outlier rather than dialect variation. The title as displayed names a different thing entirely.

title_bis "Valve sa Uga" for "Leg Vein Valves": vein in Cebuano is ugat, and the body uses it correctly ("Ang mga ugat sa imong mga tiil adunay one-way valves"). "Uga" is a different word meaning dry / dried fish, so the title reads "valve of the dried fish" and never names the vein (nor the legs). Body-vs-title mismatch confirms the title word is simply wrong, not regional.

title_bis "Dili Kayabo Adlaw" for "The Sun Isn't Fire". "Kayabo" is not a Cebuano word; fire is "kalayo" (369 corpus uses; "kayabo" appears exactly once, here). The title is the only place the card states the claim in compact form and it lands on nothing — body says "dili nagdilaab ... sama sa kandila", which is the correct wording the title should have used.

title_bis "Aurora sa Kalilum" for "Auroras Stay Silent". "Kalilum/lilom" is shade/concealment, not silence; silent is "hilom" — which the card's OWN body uses ("Kasagaran hilom ang aurora"). "Kalilum" occurs once in the whole corpus (this title) vs 128 uses of hilom/hilum, so the title is the outlier, not a dialect form.

title_bis "Dili Pareha Tuyo" for "Uneven Sun Spin". "Tuyo" in this corpus means intent/deliberate or dried fish (20 uses, none = rotation); spin is "tuyok" — the body uses "pagtuyok" and "motuyok", and 49 other titles use "tuyok". Dropped final k turns the title into a different word.

title_bis "Patong Cumulus" for "Flat Cumulus Bottoms". "Patong" means layer throughout this corpus (17 titles, e.g. "Mga Patong sa Likido", "Epidermis Gawas Patong"); flat is "patag", which is what the body uses twice ("patag nga ubos", "patag nga linya"). The title asserts a layered cumulus instead of the flat-bottom fact the card is about.

title_bis "Paghubas & Pagbanlas" for "Weathering & Erosion". "Hubas" means to dry up / ebb (all 36 corpus uses are tide going out or water drying); weathering is rendered "Pagbag-o sa Bato", "Pagguba", or "Paghugno" in every other weathering card. "Pagbanlas" for erosion is fine, so the pairing makes a Cebuano-only reader take weathering to be evaporation/low tide; the body only ever says the English "weathering", so nothing in the card corrects it.

title_bis "Ayang Tan-aw Adlaw" for "Never Stare at the Sun". "Ayang" is not a word; the negative is "ayaw" (used correctly in the body: "Ayaw gyud og tan-aw og diretso sa Adlaw!"). As printed the title reads as bare "Tan-aw Adlaw" = look at the Sun — an inverted instruction on the one eye-safety card in the batch. Body restores it, but flagging because the failure mode is a safety inversion in the most-read line.

Data defect, not a Cebuano defect: the `en` field contains the Cebuano text verbatim (identical to `bis`), so this card has no English body at all. title_en "Sun Gravity Holds Planets" is correct; the Cebuano itself is fine.

BODY defect. EN: "poles stay cold because slanted sunlight spreads thin, making the warmth weak." BIS: "Bugnaw ang mga polo sa Yuta kay HAPDOS ang kahayag sa adlaw ug mokatag..." In Cebuano hapdos = stinging/smarting pain, not slanted (hilig / pahilig). The card therefore says polar sunlight is STINGING and nothing in the card ever restores the slant — the whole causal mechanism (light arrives at an angle, so it spreads thin) is gone, replaced by a claim that contradicts the 'huyang ang init' conclusion. title_bis "Hilis Sikat Polo" is also Tagalog (hilis/sikat), so no correct word appears anywhere on the card.

TITLE defect. title_en "Sun Dogs" -> title_bis "Mga Aso sa Adlaw". Tagalog false friend: in Cebuano ASO = SMOKE (dog = iro), so the headline reads "the smokes of the sun" and names a different thing than the bright ice-crystal spots the card is about. Confirmed by this same corpus using aso = smoke correctly elsewhere (ffct-29006 'Aso nga Naipit', ffct-29007 'aso sa sakyanan', ffct-29012 'aso sa pabrika'), and the body never uses a dog word at all — it keeps the English 'sun dogs'.

TITLE defect. title_en "Mangrove Root Shields" -> title_bis "Ugat Bakawan". Tagalog false friend: Cebuano UGAT = vein/blood vessel; the root of a plant is GAMOT. The card's OWN body uses the correct word ("Ang nagkagubot nga GAMOT niini makababag sa dagkong balod"), which is the strongest evidence the title is the outlier. A child reading only the title gets 'mangrove veins'.

TITLE defect. title_en "Aluminum and Glass" -> title_bis "Aluminum ug Salamin". In Cebuano SALAMIN = mirror (glass as a material = BILDO), so the headline names a different object than the one the card is about. The body uses the correct word twice ("Ang aluminyo ug BILDO mahimong i-recycle... ang samang metal o bildo mahimong bag-ong lata o botelya"), marking the title as the outlier; the recyclable-material list is the card's whole claim, so the title mis-states it.

title_bis "Adlaw ug Bulan Laki" for "Sun & Moon Same Size": in Cebuano laki = MALE (Tagalog laki = size/bigness), so the title reads "Sun and Moon Male" and the whole point of the card — that the two LOOK almost the same size from Earth — is gone from the title. The body repeats the same Tagalogism ("halos magkasinglaki ang Adlaw ug Bulan") instead of the Cebuano gidak-on/kasingkadako, so the card never states the equal-apparent-size fact in correct Cebuano; all that survives is "bisan og mas dako gyud ang Adlaw" (the Sun is really bigger), which alone does not answer why a total solar eclipse can happen. Corpus confirms the reading: the same corpus uses "Laki nga Putyukan" for drone (male) bees and "Laki nga Lamok" for male mosquito, and uses gidak-on 349x / kasingkadako for size against only 3 uses of kasinglaki.

bis question "Ngano nga importante ang mga ulat sa intensity human sa linog?" — Cebuano ulat = SCAR (a healed-wound mark); the Tagalog ulat = report does not carry over. The card therefore asks about earthquake "scars" rather than PHIVOLCS intensity REPORTS, and no Cebuano sentence in the card ever names a report (taho/report); the answer sentences ("Nagpakita kini... Makatabang kini sa mga responder") just inherit the wrong referent, so a child learns that damage marks — not the reported intensity data — are what direct rescuers. Corpus confirms the sense: the only other corpus title using the word is "Ulat sa Hilum" = "Hilum Attachment Scar".

title_bis "Natural nga Babag" = "natural OBSTACLE/BARRIER" (babag = to block/obstruct), but the card is about natural WARNING SIGNS of a tsunami (title_en "Natural Warning Signs"). The body uses the correct word, "Unsa ang natural nga timailhan sa tsunami?" — so the title is the outlier and names a different thing. Same card's sibling (ffct-29278) correctly titles warning as "Babala", and the corpus uses babag correctly for real barriers elsewhere in this batch (ffct-29359 "Mga bukid ang mobabag sa hangin"). Corpus-wide seam: 11 other title_bis use Babag where title_en says warning (e.g. ffct-31425 "Tsunami Warnings"->"Babag sa Tsunami", ffct-30616 "Buoys Early Warning"->"Buoy Sensor Sayong Babag", ffct-32639 "Color-Coded Rain Warnings"->"Kolor nga Babag").

"Ang erosion mahitabo kung ang kusog nga ulan ug hangin MAGHANAS sa tambok nga topsoil" — hanas/kahanas in Cebuano means SKILLED / practised (corpus uses it that way ~25 times: "hanas nga mangangayam", "Kahanas sa Observing"), not "wash away". The card is a single-sentence definition of erosion, so nothing restores the meaning: a child reads that rain and wind 'train/practise' the topsoil and never learns soil is carried off. The correct verbs are used elsewhere in this same batch (ffct-29403 "aron dili kini dali nga MAANOD"; ffct-29286 "makaBANLAS").

"dalaw nagpasabot pag-amping, kahel nagpasabot pangandam, ug pula nagpasabot mobakwit" — YELLOW is rendered as "dalaw", which is not a colour word in Cebuano (yellow = dalag, or dilaw/dulaw; "dalaw" reads as Tagalog for a visit). The whole point of the card is the three-colour->three-action mapping, and the first pair is broken with no recovery anywhere in the card: a child cannot learn which rainfall warning colour means 'be aware'. Corpus uses dalag 232x and the parallel card ffct-29804 uses "dilaw, orange, ug pula"; this is the only "dalaw" colour hit in the whole corpus.

title_bis "Kapeckan sa Bagyo" for title_en "Typhoon Hazards Beyond Wind": "kapeckan" is not a Cebuano word (the 'ck' cluster does not occur in Cebuano orthography) and it is the only content word in the title, so the title says nothing — it does not resolve to kapeligrohan, katalagman or any guessable word. Never appears in any card body corpus-wide, only in 7 titles, so it is a generation artifact rather than regional usage. Body is fine and delivers the fact; the title is unreadable.

title_bis "Signal 4 sa Kapeckan" — same non-word as ffct-29335 standing in for danger/hazard (title_en "Signal Number 4"). Not Cebuano and not recoverable by a reader; body ("grabe ka kusog ug makaguba nga hangin... sulod sa mga 12 ka oras") is correct, so only the title is defective.

title_bis "Groundwater sa Balon" — Tagalog false friend: balon is Tagalog for "well", but in Cebuano balon = provisions/food taken on a trip (a well is atabay or bubon). The card's own body uses the correct word ("makuha nato sa atabay ug tuburan"), which marks the title as the outlier; the title as written labels the card with a different thing entirely.

title_bis "Red Giant Uma" for title_en "Future Red Giant Sun" — "uma" is Cebuano for FARM/field (it is used correctly with that meaning in ffct-29528's title "Konstelasyon Uma" in this same batch). It appears to be a truncation of "umaabot" (future), leaving a star card labelled "Red Giant Farm".

title_bis "Adlaw sa Gabii ug Tirok" for title_en "Night and Earth's Turning" — tirok means to gather/congregate in Cebuano, not to rotate; rotation is tuyok. The body uses the right word ("Nagtuyok lang ang Yuta"), so the title is the outlier and names a different concept than the card teaches.

title_bis "Lalim nga Mahimong Fossil" for "Fossils Are Rare". In Cebuano "lalim" means EASY (the everyday phrase "dili lalim" = not easy); read as Tagalog it means depth. Either way the title asserts the opposite of, or nothing about, rarity. The card's own body has it right ("Panagsa ra mahimong fossil"), and the corpus uses talagsaon/panagsa for rare elsewhere, so the title is the outlier. Same swap recurs in ffct-29065 ("Gems Are Rare" -> "Lalim nga mga Hiyas").

title_bis "Limestone ug Bingkil" for "Limestone and Seashells". Cebuano "bingkil" means a quarrel/falling-out, not a shell; shell is kabibe or kabhang - which is exactly what this card's own body uses twice ("mga kabibe", "kabhang"). The title therefore names a different thing than the English. Same swap appears in ffct-10315 ("Shells Protect Clams" -> "Bingkil Tahong", body again uses kabhang), so it is a systematic wrong word, not a regional variant.

title_bis "Ang Bulawan Dili Makaunod" for "Gold Never Rusts". "Unod" is flesh/meat/contents; "dili makaunod" says nothing about rusting, so the title's claim is unreadable rather than true. The body has the correct word ("dili magkalawang"), and across ~250 rust cards the corpus consistently uses taya/kalawang - "makaunod" occurs only in this one card, marking the title as the defect.

title_bis "Edad sa Kalibutan" for "Age of the Universe", with the body giving 13.8 billion years. "Kalibutan" is the world/Earth, and this same batch uses it that way twice (ffct-29705 "71% Tubig sa Kalibutan" = Earth's surface; ffct-29655 "presyur sulod sa Kalibutan" = inside the Earth). A child reading the title plus the number is set up to believe the Earth is 13.8 billion years old; the body's word "uniberso" is the correct one and is what the title should have used.

title_bis "Aurora sa Ekwador" (Aurora at the Equator) states the OPPOSITE of the card: EN title is "Auroras Near the Poles" and the body says auroras are seen near the north/south poles and usually NOT here because we are near the equator. A child reading the heading alone learns that auroras happen at the equator. Same card's body also uses "poste sa Kalibutan" for the poles (poste = post/pillar); the corpus's own correct word is "polo" (ffct-29876: "sa mga polo").

"kahayag sa langit duol sa mga poste sa Kalibutan" — poste in Cebuano is a POST/PILLAR (lamppost), not a geographic pole (polo). Nothing else in this card restores it: no amihanan/habagatan, no polo. The card's single locating fact (auroras occur near Earth's poles) is unrecoverable; the child reads "near the Earth's posts". ffct-29876 in the same batch uses "polo" correctly, so poste is the outlier.

Tagalog false friend in title_bis "Rainbow sa Talon". Tagalog talon = waterfall; Cebuano talon = to jump/leap (waterfall is busay). The card's OWN body uses the correct word — "sa tinilamsik sa busay, tubod, o hose" — which is the strongest evidence the title is the outlier. Heading reads "Rainbow at the Jump".

title_bis "Pagbuto sa Bahaghari" = "The EXPLOSION of the Rainbow" (Cebuano buto = explode/burst; buto-as-seed is the Tagalog sense). The English is "How Rainbows Form", and the card's own body uses the correct word twice — "Unsaon pagporma sa balangaw? / Maporma kini...". The title names a different event than the card teaches.

title_bis "Butkon ug Kurug sa Kulog" — butkon is bukton, the ARM, not a thunder crack; kurug is a shiver/tremble, not a rumble. The heading reads "Arm and Shiver of Thunder". The body has both correct words ("hait nga putok" for the crack, "taas nga lagubo" for the rumble), so the title is the outlier and names a different thing entirely.

title_bis "Nagsapaw nga mga Plaka" = OVERLAPPING/stacked plates (sapaw = to overlay), which is the convergent/subduction picture, not the transform boundary the card is about. The body uses the correct verb "maglampasanay ... sa magkasumpaki nga direksyon". The heading alone teaches the wrong plate relationship.

title_bis "Clay nga Lipad-lipad" — lipad/lupad is FLYING, not slippery; the card's key property (clay turns danlog, slippery, when waterlogged) is missing from the heading, which instead names flight. Body uses the correct word: "mahimo kining danlog sama sa sabon". Lower severity than the others (the heading is nonsense rather than false), but it is a title wrong-word with the correct word present in the same card.

title_bis "Ang Kulog Tunod Ra" — tunod in Cebuano is to sink/set (as the sun does), so the heading loses the card's entire point ("Thunder Is Just Sound"). Almost certainly a slip for tunog; the body carries the correct Cebuano "Ang dalugdog tingog ra". Flagged because the whole claim lives in the title and the word that lands there means something else.

Body: "wala-mabordahi nga porselana" = UN-EMBROIDERED porcelain (borda = embroidery). English is "unglazed porcelain tile", the one property that defines a streak plate. Nothing else in the card mentions glaze, so the defining property is unrecoverable from the Cebuano.

title_bis "Katinig sa Mineral" — katinig is Tagalog for CONSONANT; Cebuano for hardness is katig-a. The card's own body uses "katig-a" correctly, and sibling cards ffct-29998/ffct-29999 title it "Tig-a"/"Katig-a", so the title is the outlier.
title_bis "Mohs Scale sa Katinig" — same Tagalog false friend: katinig = consonant, not hardness (katig-a). Body uses "katig-a" twice; title names a different thing.
title_bis "Pagkalot nga Test sa Katinig" — katinig (Tagalog: consonant) again used for hardness; the body correctly says "katig-a", confirming the title word is the defect.

title_bis "Bukid nga Mokatul pa" — katul/katol in Cebuano is to ITCH, so the title reads "mountains that still itch". English is "Mountains Still Rising"; the body's "nagtaas" is the correct word and shows the title is wrong.
title_bis "Bulawan nga Dili Makaunod" — unod is flesh/meat; "makaunod" names nothing like rust (taya / kalawang). The body's "dili magkalawang" is correct, so the title is the outlier.

title_bis "Hinaw nga Kusog" — hinaw in Cebuano is to WASH (one's hands), not clean-as-adjective (hinlo/limpyo). Body says "limpyo nga enerhiya" and sibling card ffct-29981 titles it "Hinlo nga Geothermal Energy", so the title word is wrong for "clean" in general.

title_bis "Kahuol ug Pananom" — kahuol is anguish/breathlessness, not drought (huwaw/hulaw). The English title is "Droughts and Crops" and the body correctly uses "huwaw"; the title never names the drought.

title_bis "Mga Ugat nga Stilt" for "Mangrove Stilt Roots" — in Cebuano ugat is a VEIN/blood vessel (Tagalog false friend for root); the heading reads "stilt veins". The card's own body and emph_bis use the correct Cebuano gamot ("tag-as nga mga gamot nga morag tukod"), and the terms list carries the Tagalog form "ugat na nakatayo" beside gamot — so the title is the outlier. Corpus evidence: this same card set uses ugat for LEAF VEINS (ffct-04128 "Ugat sa Dahon"), and plant roots are gamot 462x vs ugat 39x, the ugat hits being almost all titles.

title_bis "Ugat nga Moginhawa" for "Breathing Roots" — reads as "breathing veins" in Cebuano, naming a different organ than the card is about. Body uses gamot twice ("Unsaon pagginhawa sa mga gamot sa bakhaw...", "ang ubang gamot mosulbong pataas"), and the terms list pairs Tagalog "ugat na humihinga" with Cebuano "gamot nga ginhawa", so the Tagalog word leaked into the title only. Same systematic title defect as ffct-30163.

title_bis "Hamas nga Buto" for "Smooth Rounded Grains": `buto` is the Tagalog word for seed/bone; in Cebuano `buto` means an explosion/burst (and is vulgar slang), so the title names a different thing than the card is about. The card's own body uses the correct Cebuano word `lugas` ("Kung mas dugay nga giligid sa balud ang usa ka lugas, mas pino, lingin, ug hamis kini"), which is the evidence that the title is the outlier rather than regional variation. `Hamas` is also not a word (should be `hamis`, smooth), so the whole title fails to name the grain. Title-only defect; the body still delivers the fact.

title_en "Morning Dew" but title_bis = "Gabon sa Buntag" — gabon is FOG, not dew. The card's own body uses the right word ("Ang yamog mao ang gagmayng tinulo sa tubig nga makita sa sagbot ug mga dahon kada buntag"), so the title is the outlier, and the sibling card in this same batch (ffct-30361) exists specifically to teach that fog and dew are NOT the same ("ang gabon maporma sa hangin mismo, samtang ang yamog maporma sa ibabaw sa mga butang"). A Cebuano-only child reading the heading is taught the exact conflation the neighbouring card corrects. Corpus cross-check: every other dew title uses yamog/hamog (Yamog sa Dahon, Hamog sa Gabii, Punto sa Hamog); this is the only gabon-titled dew card.

title_en "Fog, a Ground Cloud" → title_bis "Yabo nga Panganod". In Cebuano yabo = to spill/pour out, not fog; the title reads "spilled cloud". The card's own body uses the correct word throughout ("Ang gabon usa ka panganod nga naporma sa yuta"), which is the evidence the title is the outlier. Corpus cross-check: yabo is used for SPILLING in Cebuano bodies elsewhere ("nayabo nga asido sa lab", "dili kini mayabo", "ang pag-yabo sa tubig gikan sa mga sudlanan"), and appears as "fog" ONLY in generated titles — the same broken title family also produced "Yabo Ulap Yuta" (ffct-28986) and "Dili Kayabo Adlaw" (ffct-28965, for "The Sun Isn't Fire", i.e. kalayo mangled). Systematic, ~8 cards corpus-wide.

title_en "What Fog Is Made of" → title_bis "Sulod sa Yabo" = "inside the spill". Same defect family as ffct-30354: yabo is spill, fog is gabon, and this card's own body says gabon correctly ("Ang gabon gilangkuban sa daghan kaayong gagmayng tinulo sa tubig"). The child cannot connect the heading to the card.

title_en "Thick Fog on Roads" → title_bis "Yabo sa Dalan" = "a spill on the road" — which in a road-safety card reads as a real and different hazard (spilled liquid), not fog. Body is correct Cebuano ("Sa baga nga gabon, lisod makita ang halayo nga mga butang"), so the title alone carries the wrong thing; of the three yabo cards in this batch this is the one where the wrong word is independently plausible and therefore most likely to be believed.

EN "What scale do scientists use for really big earthquakes today? ... For huge earthquakes, scientists now use the moment magnitude scale (Mw)" becomes "para sa daghan kaayong mga linog" / "Para sa daghang mga linog" = "for VERY MANY earthquakes". Size is swapped for quantity in BOTH the question and the answer, and title_bis ("Moment sa Magnitude") does not restore it: the card never says dako/kusog anywhere. A Cebuano-only reader learns that Mw is the scale used when there are many earthquakes, which is false and leaves the real fact (Mw is for the largest quakes) unrecoverable. Cebuano daghan = many/numerous; big = dako.

"Sinking Land in Manila" -> title_bis "Nalubog nga Yuta sa Manila" and body "naglubog usab ang yuta". Tagalog lubog = submerged/sinking, but Cebuano lubog = murky/turbid (lubog nga tubig); to sink is lunod/unlod. The card's whole fact is that Manila's land is subsiding, and nothing in the card restores it — read as Cebuano the sentence becomes "the land is also getting murky, so the sea seems to rise faster", which does not deliver subsidence. Corpus-internal evidence that lubog is the outlier: sibling cards use the correct word for submersion (ffct-30542 "mahimong malunod", ffct-30543 "kung malunod ang baybayon").

EN "Cumulus look like fluffy cotton balls" -> "Ang cumulus murag humok nga bulak". Tagalog bulak = cotton, but Cebuano bulak = FLOWER (cotton in Cebuano is gapas). The card never corrects it, so a Cebuano-only reader is told cumulus clouds look like soft flowers rather than cotton balls — a different object, and the comparison is the only content the card gives for cumulus. Honest caveat: "humok" still conveys softness, so the fluffiness survives even though the named object does not.

EN "The Moon's pull causes ocean tides to rise and fall" -> BIS "Ang birik sa Bulan maoy hinungdan sa pagtaob ug paghunas sa dagat". In Cebuano 'birik' is to spin/rotate (bira/guyod/hila = pull; gravity = grabidad), so a Cebuano-only child is taught that the Moon's SPIN drives the tides - a different mechanism from gravitational pull, and the misconception the card exists to prevent. Nothing in the card corrects it: the title is just "Bulan ug Tides" and 'birik' is the emph_bis highlight, so it is the word the UI pushes at the child. The corpus's own sibling card on the same fact says it correctly - ffct-02394: "Ang gravity sa Bulan mao ang nag-unang hinungdan sa tides" - which is what makes this card the outlier. Confidence low-to-medium: 'birik' appears only 3x in the whole corpus and all 3 render English "pull" (ffct-16313 "birik sa grabidad", ffct-32028 "birik sa Adlaw"), so this looks like one translator's systematic (and I believe wrong) choice rather than a one-off slip; if a native speaker accepts 'birik' for gravitational attraction, all three cards pass together.

title_bis "Yabo nga Panganod sa Yuta" for "Fog, a Ground Cloud": Cebuano *yabo* means to spill/pour out (corpus uses it that way in ffct-15651 "sa pagyabo", ffct-08616 "pag-yabo sa tubig", ffct-25761 "dili mayabo ang tubig"), not fog. The card's OWN body uses the correct word — "Ang gabon morag panganod nga naglingkod sa yuta" — so the title is the outlier. Systematic: 234.json ffct-34846 titles "Fog in Baguio" as "Yabo sa Baguio" too. A child reading the title learns fog = yabo, which is false vocabulary for the card's own subject.

title_bis "Liwat sa mga Panganod" for "Clouds Move with Wind": Cebuano *liwat* means to resemble / take after (kaliwat = breed, lineage, descendants — see ffct-04650, ffct-03948, ffct-13087 in this corpus), not movement, which is *lihok*. The card's own body uses the right word ("Nagalupad ug naglihok ang mga panganod kay gidala sa hangin"), so the title names a different thing than the English. Systematic across titles: ffct-24165 "Inertia sa Pundo ug Liwat" (Motion), ffct-12559 "Adlaw-adlaw nga Liwat sa Bata" (Daily Activity), ffct-11361 "Kusang ug Tuyo nga Liwat" (Moves) — all with bodies that correctly say lihok.

title_bis "Bihag Ra Fossil" uses bihag = CAPTIVE/taken prisoner for English "rare". The title reads "Only captive fossils" — a different claim from "fossilization is rare". The card's OWN body uses the correct word ("Talagsaon ra kini"), and terms lists talagsaon, so the title is the outlier. Confirmed false-friend class (Tagalog bihira/bihag confusion).

title_bis "Babag sa Ubos nga Signal" uses babag = OBSTACLE/blockage where English is "warning" (Early Low-Signal Warnings). Title reads "Obstruction at the low signal" — names a different thing and also drops the "early/lead time" point that is the whole card. Body uses the correct word pasidaan throughout, so the title is the outlier.

title_bis "Hydrogen nga Sobra sa Adlaw" = "excess/left-over hydrogen in the Sun", but the card is "Hydrogen Fuels the Sun". Sobra (excess) is not fuel; a child reading the title is told the Sun has surplus hydrogen rather than that hydrogen is its fuel. Body uses the correct word sugnod (and terms list sugnod/gatong), so the title is the outlier.

title_bis "Tirok sa Yuta pakadto" is both a wrong word and truncated: tirok = to GATHER/congregate, not to spin (tuyok/libot), and "pakadto" (going toward) is left with no destination, so the card's entire fact — west to east — is missing from the title. Body has it right ("Molibot ang Earth gikan sa kasadpan paingon sa sidlakan").

"gikan sa nabulok nga mga tanom ug hayop" uses bulok, which in Cebuano means COLOUR (and dull-witted), not rotten — that is Tagalog. Correct Cebuano is nadunot/nalata (the card's own terms list has madunot). Nothing else in the Cebuano supplies the decay idea, so the source of soil carbon (decayed plants and animals) is lost.

"gibulok sila sa decomposer sama sa bakterya ug fungi" — bulok = COLOUR in Cebuano (Tagalog false friend for rotten/decayed); correct is gidunot/gilata/gadugmok. This is the card's only verb for "break them down", and no other Cebuano word in the card restores it, so the decomposition mechanism itself is not stated in Cebuano. The terms list carries the correct madunot.

title_bis "Karaang Kinabuhi Fue" ends in the non-word "Fue" — a truncated "Fuel"/"Fuels". The title therefore never says what the card is about (fossil fuels); it reads "Ancient Life Fue". Not register or compact style — the word is cut off. Body is correct ("fossil fuels ang langis, gas, ug karbon").

Tagalog false friend in the body's central comparison. EN: "Why do some hot springs smell like rotten eggs?" BIS: "Ngano ang ubang hot spring mobaho sama sa BULOK nga itlog?" In Cebuano bulok = COLOUR (unsa'y bulok sa imong sinina?); rotten egg is bugok nga itlog (general rot = dunot/lata). The card reads "smells like a coloured egg", and nothing in the card restores "rotten" — the answer only says the water picks up the smell from sulfur-rich rocks. The whole point of the card is the rotten-egg smell cue for sulfur, so a Cebuano-only child loses the fact the card depends on. Note the corpus uses kolor correctly for colour in the neighbouring card ffct-31283 ("Kolor sa Hot Spring"), which is evidence bulok here is the outlier, not a dialect choice.

Direction reversal in the question, plus a dropped negation in the answer. EN: "Could a black hole swallow Earth?" BIS: "Mahimo bang TUKBON SA YUTA ang black hole?" — in Cebuano patient-focus, the sa-phrase is the agent and the ang-phrase the patient, so this asks "Can the EARTH swallow the BLACK HOLE?", the exact opposite. Correct would be "Matukob/Mahurot ba sa black hole ang Yuta?". The answer does not repair it and adds a second problem: "layo kaayo NGA makabira sa Yuta" uses the Cebuano "X kaayo nga Y" result construction, so it reads "so far away THAT IT CAN pull the Earth" — the English "too far TO pull Earth" needs a negative/purpose form (e.g. "layo ra kaayo para makabira sa Yuta" or "dili na makabira sa Yuta"). A Cebuano-only child gets a reversed question and an answer that literally affirms the black hole can pull Earth.

title_bis "Hinaw nga Tubig sa Bukal" for "Clear Spring Water". Classic Tagalog false friend: TL bukal = spring, but Cebuano bukal = to BOIL (pabukala ang tubig); a water source is tuburan — which this card's OWN body uses correctly ("pag mogawas sa tuburan"), the strongest sign the title is the outlier. Compounding it, "hinaw" is hand-washing water in Cebuano, not "clear" (tin-aw). The title reads "wash-water from the boiling" — a different thing from clear spring water, and it is never corrected in the title's own terms.

title_bis "Babag sa Tsunami" = "tsunami barrier/blockade" for title_en "Tsunami Warnings". The card is entirely about detection and alerting (sensors, "mopadala og pasidaan aron makabiya dayon ang mga tawo"), never about physical barriers — a sea wall is a genuinely different thing from a warning system. The body uses the correct word (pasidaan), and the same batch uses babag correctly for a real barrier in ffct-31482 ("Babag sa Bukid" = Mountain Barriers), confirming this title is the outlier.

title_bis "Pagbuto sa Lanaw" = "the exploding/bursting of the lake" for title_en "How Lakes Form". In Cebuano mobuto/pagbuto is to explode; there is no reading that means "to form". The card's mechanism is the opposite of explosive — a hollow left by ice, a volcano or shifting land quietly filling with rain, streams or groundwater — and the body uses the correct word ("Maporma ang lanaw kung mapuno og tubig..."), so the title names an event the card never describes.

bis: "sulfur gas nga baho og bulok nga itlog" for EN "smells like rotten eggs". In Cebuano bulok = COLOUR (rotten is dunot/lata); this is the confirmed Tagalog false friend. The card's whole identifying hook is the rotten-egg smell and nothing in the card restores it — terms even carry 'rotten egg'/'amoy itlog' but the body never says dunot. A Cebuano-only reader gets 'smells like a coloured egg' and cannot answer what sulfur gas smells like.

bis: "mas init ang gabii kon humok ang hangin" for EN "It makes humid nights feel warmer". humok = SOFT in Cebuano (606 uses elsewhere in this corpus are all 'soft', incl. ffct-31604 'humok nga klase' of coal); humid is halumigmig/umog — the corpus uses 'umog' correctly in ffct-31549/31553. The card never corrects it, so the water-vapour/humidity link becomes the nonsense claim that nights are warmer when the air is soft.

title_bis "Lumot Talc Papel" uses lumot for English "Soft" (title_en: Soft Talc Leaves Mark). In Cebuano lumot = MOSS/algae, not soft; soft is humok — which is exactly what this card's own body uses ("humok kaayo ang Talc"). The title tells a Cebuano child the card is about mossy talc.

title_bis "Soapstone Marka Bakal" uses bakal for "Metal" (title_en: Talc Marks Metal Factories). bakal in Cebuano = TO BUY; iron/metal is puthaw — the card's own body says "Unsaon pagmarka sa puthaw" and "marka sa puthaw". Title reads as "soapstone mark buy", so the metal-marking subject is gone from the title.

title_bis "Composting Balat Prutas Pataba" uses balat for fruit peel. In Cebuano balat = SEA CUCUMBER (the marine animal); peel/skin is panit, which the card's own body uses correctly ("panit sa prutas"). Title reads as sea-cucumber-fruit compost. (pataba for fertilizer is also Tagalog vs the body's abono, but that one is recoverable; balat is the naming error.)

The card's entire point is TWO distinct motions, but the Cebuano uses libot (orbit/go around) for both. EN: stars slide east-west nightly "because Earth spins" -> BIS "tungod kay molibot ang Earth"; then the monthly swap -> "paglibot sa Earth sa Adlaw". Corpus convention confirms the split (ffct-31707 "nagtuyok ang Kalibutan" = spins; ffct-31746/31762 "molibot ang Earth sa Adlaw" = orbits), and ffct-31778 rescues the same slip with "pagtuyok" — this card never does. A Cebuano-only reader concludes Earth's orbit causes the nightly east-to-west motion (false) and cannot name the two moves the title "Duha ka Lihok" promises. Fix: "tungod kay motuyok ang Earth".

title_bis "Bakal Core Magnetic Poles" uses bakal, which in Cebuano means TO BUY, not iron (puthaw). The card's own body uses the correct word — "natunaw nga puthaw sa outer core" — so the title is the outlier: the heading names a different thing (buying) than "Molten Iron Poles" and is never corrected within the title itself. This is the confirmed bakal false-friend pattern, in the title, with body evidence against it.

NUMBER CHANGED. EN: "365 and a quarter days"; BIS: "mokabat og mga 365 ug tunga ka adlaw" = 365 and a HALF days. 'tunga' is half, not a quarter. This also breaks the card's own logic: a half-day surplus would need an extra day every 2 years, not the "matag ikaupat ka tuig" the very next sentence states. A child reading only the Cebuano learns a wrong orbital period and a leap-year rule that does not follow from it. Nothing in the card restores the quarter.

RELATIONSHIP REVERSED in the Q/A. EN: "Are weathering and erosion the same thing? | Nope!". BIS flips the question but keeps the answer: "Lahi ba ang weathering ug erosion? | Dili!" = "Are weathering and erosion DIFFERENT? | No!" — i.e. the card explicitly tells the child the two ARE the same, which is precisely the misconception the card exists to correct. Every other Dili!-card in this batch (ffct-31987, -32009, -32026, -32055, -32078, -32106) keeps the polarity intact, so this one is the outlier, not a house style.

TAGALOG FALSE FRIEND IN TITLE. title_en "Plastic Never Rots" -> title_bis "Plastik nga Dili Mabulok". 'mabulok' is Tagalog for rot; in Cebuano 'bulok' is not rot (dull/colour sense), so the title does not deliver "does not rot" at all. The card's OWN body uses the correct Cebuano: "Ang plastik dili madunot sama sa dahon o pagkaon" — strongest evidence the title is the defect. Fix: "Plastik nga Dili Madunot".

TAGALOG FALSE FRIEND IN TITLE, same defect as ffct-32019. title_en "Microplastics Never Rot" -> title_bis "Dili Mabulok nga Plastik". Body uses the correct Cebuano verb in both question and answer ("Madunot ba o matunaw ang microplastics...? | Dili!"), so the title is the outlier. Fix: "Dili Madunot nga Plastik".

Body changes the hiding mechanism from muddy/murky water to COLD water and never corrects it. EN: "Mangrove water is muddy and shady! Big fish can't see tiny fish in this murky water." BIS: "Mabugnaw ug malandong ang tubig sa bakawan! Dili makita sa dagkong isda ang gagmay nga isda sa mabugnaw nga tubig." mabugnaw = cold; the needed word is malubog (murky) / lapok. The wrong word appears twice and is the highlighted phrase (emph_bis = 'Mabugnaw ug malandong'), so a child learns (a) mangrove water is cold - contradicting ffct-32162 in the same batch, "motubo lang sa init ug parat nga baybayon" - and (b) that coldness is why predators cannot see the fry. title_bis 'Lapok nga Tagoanan' is correct, which is what identifies the body as the outlier; the closing line mentions lapok only as an *extra* hiding spot, so the murky-water fact itself is never delivered.

Time zones are attributed to Earth's REVOLUTION instead of its rotation. EN: "Because Earth rotates!" BIS: "Kay molibot ang Earth!" - molibot = to go around / orbit; rotation is motuyok / magtuyok. The same batch fixes both meanings: ffct-32220 uses molibot for orbiting the Sun ("ang Earth maoy molibot sa Adlaw") and ffct-32126 uses tuyok for spinning ("nagatuyok nga poste"), so in this corpus molibot unambiguously reads as orbit. emph_bis highlights 'molibot', and nothing else in the card mentions spinning, so a child ends up with the classic rotation/revolution misconception - that different countries have different clock times because Earth travels around the Sun.

title_bis "Hinay nga Pagbuto sa Yuta" = "the soil's slow EXPLOSION" (buto = blow up; the same batch uses "mibuto" for Pinatubo erupting). English title is "Slow Soil Formation", and the card's own body has the correct word — "Hinay kaayo ang pagporma sa yuta". Classic title-outlier: the body says pagporma, only the heading says pagbuto.

Body: "topsoil sa ibabaw, subsoil SA KINAADMAN, ug solid bedrock sa pinakaubos". Kinaadman = wisdom/knowledge, not a place; the English is "subsoil is below it" (ilawom / kahiladman — likely a corruption of kahiladman, "the depths"). This card's whole point is the ORDER of the layers, and the middle layer's position word is nonsense; a child can only infer it from the list order.

Tagalog false friend: "puti nga parehas sa BULAK" — Tagalog bulak = cotton, but Cebuano bulak = FLOWER (cotton in Cebuano is gapas). English is "puffy and white just like cotton". Nothing else in the card mentions cotton, so the image a Cebuano child gets is a flower, not cotton. (terms[] even carries the pair "cotton"/"bulak", so the swap is baked in.)

title_bis "Mainit nga Dagat nga Sobra" = "warm sea that is excess/extra"; English title is "Warm Seas as Fuel" and sobra is not fuel (sugnod/gasolina). Lower confidence than the others because the body does restore the idea ("sama sa gasolina niini ... mawad-an kini sa gasolina") — flagged only because the defect is in the title, where the concept the heading is built on is replaced by a different word.

Go-bag contents list "pagkain, tubig, gamot, importante nga dokumento, ug flashlight" — English is "medicine". In Cebuano gamot = ROOT (medicine = tambal), the confirmed false friend, and nothing else in the card restores "medicine". Same-batch evidence: ffct-32495 ("Roots Hold the Soil") uses gamot correctly for roots, so this corpus really does mean root by gamot. A child packing a go-bag from this card loses the medicine item.

"Sa ting-init ... mohuyop ang hangin gikan sa dagat. Sa ting-ulan, mas mainit ang dagat mao nga mag-reverse ang hangin" — English says "In winter, warmer sea reverses the wind". Ting-ulan is the RAINY season, not winter (tingtugnaw, which ffct-32537 in this same batch uses correctly for winter). The card therefore puts the monsoon reversal in the wet season, i.e. exactly when the habagat blows in FROM the sea — a reversed season/direction fact that nothing in the card corrects, and it contradicts ffct-32463 (amihan = Dec-Feb).

title_bis "Dali Mabulok nga Kaon" for "Fast Food Spoilage". Bulok in Cebuano = COLOUR (the confirmed false friend; spoil/rot = madunot). The card's OWN body uses the correct word twice ("paspas madunot ang pagkain", "pagkadunot"), which marks the title as the outlier rather than regional variation. Title as shipped reads "quickly-coloured eating", not "food spoils fast".

title_bis "Matabang Floodplain" for "Fertile Floodplains". Matabang is the Tagalog import (lupang mataba/matabang = fertile); in Cebuano it reads as bland/tasteless (tab-ang) or helpful (tabang), never fertile — Cebuano fertile soil is tabunok. Lower severity than the three above: title-only, and the body paraphrases the idea as "maayo kaayo nga farmland tungod sa rich sediment" without ever using tabunok.

EN folk sign is 'many ants moving means rain is coming'; bis says 'daghang langgam nga nagbalhin nagpasabot og ulan'. In Cebuano langgam = BIRD (ant = hulmigas/guyam) — the confirmed Tagalog false friend. Nothing in the card corrects it, and the terms list even carries the bad mapping ("ants", "langgam"), so a child learns a different weather sign (migrating birds) than the card teaches.

Q&A card: the Cebuano question asks 'Nganong importante kaayo nga magpabilin ang mga kahoy ug balili sa mga bukid?' but the answer only states that heavy rain on steep slopes strips topsoil via erosion. The EN answer's second sentence — 'Trees and grass hold the soil in place' — is dropped entirely, so the Cebuano never links trees/grass to holding soil and the card's own question is left unanswered.

EN: the second rainbow 'has its colors in reverse order'. Bis says 'binalikbalik ang ayos sa kolor', which reads as the order being repeated/done over and over, not reversed (Cebuano for reversed is balit-ad/baliktad — this same corpus uses 'balit-ad' correctly in ffct-32613). The reversal is the card's distinguishing fact and nothing else in the card restores it. Lower confidence than the other two: a sympathetic reader may still take 'balik' as 'flipped back'.

EN: andesite "can produce more explosive eruptions".
